inline.s: Adorning all their practices, their standards were complete. They contemplated dharmas as illusions, ever still in samadhi. Guarding well the karma of speech, they did not censure the faults of others; guarding well the karma of body, they never lost their precepts; guarding well the karma of mind, they were pure and undefiled. To all cities, villages, kinsmen, and treasures they were utterly unattached. Always by the six perfections of giving, precepts, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom, they taught and established sentient beings, causing them to abide in the supreme, true Way.

Because such roots of good had been accomplished, wherever they were born, immeasurable treasures naturally responded. Sometimes they were elders or householders, of noble and honored family; sometimes khattiya kings or wheel-turning sages; sometimes lords of the six heavens of desire, even up to the brahma kings. At the places of the Buddhas they paid respect and made offerings without interruption. Such merit and virtue cannot be fully spoken.

From their bodies and mouths they always emitted immeasurable wondrous fragrance, like sandalwood (zhan) and the utpala flower, their scent perfuming immeasurable worlds. Wherever born, their form and appearance were upright and dignified, endowed with the thirty-two marks and the eighty minor features. From their hands there always issued inexhaustible treasures and ornaments, all necessities, the supreme objects, for the benefit and joy of all beings. Through this cause, they can cause immeasurable sentient beings to bring forth the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

blocks.text: Chapter Nine: The Accomplishment of Perfection

inline.s: The Buddha told Ananda: The monk Dharmakara, practicing the bodhisattva's course and accumulating merit and virtue, was immeasurable and boundless. In all dharmas he attained freedom, beyond what words and discrimination can know. The vows he set forth were accomplished in perfection; he truly abided, endowed with adornment, majestic virtue, and power in a pure Buddha land.

Ananda, hearing what the Buddha had said, asked the World-Honored One: The bodhisattva Dharmakara who attained enlightenment, was he a Buddha of the past, or a Buddha of the future? Or is he now in another world in the present?

The World-Honored One replied: That Thus-Come One came from nowhere and goes to nowhere; he is without arising and without ceasing, not past, future, or present. But in fulfillment of his vows to deliver beings, he now dwells in the west, ten thousand kotis of Buddha lands from here, in a world called Sukhavati. Dharmakara became a Buddha, named Amitabha. Since his enlightenment ten aeons have passed. Now he teaches the Dharma, surrounded with respect by immeasurable, countless bodhisattvas and hearers.

blocks.text: Chapter Ten: All Aspire to Become Buddhas

inline.s: The Buddha spoke of Amitabha Buddha's vows attained when he was a bodhisattva. At that time, Ajatashatru the crown prince and five hundred sons of elders, hearing it, all rejoiced greatly, and each holding a golden flower-canopy, came to the Buddha and bowed. After offering the canopies over the Buddha, they sat to one side to hear the scripture, and wished in their hearts: May we, when we become Buddhas, all be like Amitabha Buddha.

The Buddha, knowing this, told the monks: These princes and the rest shall in the future become Buddhas. In former lives they dwelt on the bodhisattva path, and for countless aeons made offerings to forty kotis of Buddhas. In the time of Kasyapa Buddha they were my disciples; now they make offerings to me and meet me again. At that time the monks who heard the Buddha's words did not fail to rejoice on their behalf.

blocks.text: Chapter Eleven: The Pure and Adorned Land

inline.s: The Buddha told Ananda: That land of Sukhavati, with immeasurable merit and virtue, is fully adorned. Forever there is no name for the many sufferings, the many calamities, the evil destinies, or the afflictions of maras. Nor is there the difference of the four seasons, of cold and heat, or of rain and gloom. Further, there are no great or small rivers, no hills and pits, no thorns and gravel, no iron-ring mountains, no Sumeru, and no mountains of earth or stone. Only naturally, with the seven jewels and gold for its ground, it is vast and even, without measure or limit. Subtle and wondrous, pure and adorned, it surpasses all the worlds of the ten directions.
Ananda, hearing this, asked the World-Honored One: If that land has no Mount Sumeru, upon what do the four heavens of the kings and the Trayastrimsa heaven depend?
The Buddha told Ananda: Upon what do the Yama, Tushita, and even the heavens of the form and formless realms, all the devas, depend?
Ananda replied: It is owing to their inconceivable karmic power.

The Buddha told Ananda: Can you know this inconceivable karma? The retribution of your own body is inconceivable; the karma of sentient beings is inconceivable; the roots of good of sentient beings are inconceivable; the sagely power of the Buddhas and the worlds of the Buddhas are also inconceivable. The beings of that land, by the power of their merit and virtue, abide in the stage of their practice, and by the Buddha's spiritual power, are able to be so.

Ananda said: The karma, cause, and retribution are inconceivable! In this Dharma I truly have no doubt. But for the sake of future sentient beings, to break the net of their doubt, I ask this question.

blocks.text: Chapter Twelve: The Light Shines Everywhere

inline.s: The Buddha told Ananda: The majestic power of Amitabha Buddha's light is most honored and supreme. The Buddhas of the ten directions cannot match it. It shines throughout the Buddha lands of the eastern Ganges-sands, and likewise south, west, and north, the four directions, above and below. If it is the halo on his head, it may be one, two, three, or four yojanas, or a hundred, a thousand, a koti, or a kotinayuta of yojanas. The lights of the Buddhas may illumine one or two Buddha lands, or a hundred or a thousand. Only Amitabha Buddha's light shines universally throughout immeasurable, countless, boundless Buddha lands.

The distance to which the lights of the Buddhas reach depends on the meritorious vows they made when seeking the Way in former lives, and their merits differ in greatness. When they become Buddhas, each attains accordingly. It is of itself, not by prior calculation.

Amitabha Buddha's light is good and excellent, surpassing the brightness of the sun and moon a thousand kotis and tens of millions of times. The most honored within light, the king of Buddhas. Therefore Amitabha Buddha is also called the Buddha of Immeasurable Light, also the Buddha of Boundless Light, Unhindered Light, Uncomparable Light; also the Buddha of Wisdom Light, Ever-Shining Light, Pure Light, Joyful Light, Liberating Light, Tranquil Light, Light Surpassing Sun and Moon, and the Light of the Inconceivable.

Such a light shines universally upon the ten directions and all worlds. Those sentient beings who encounter this light, their defilements are extinguished, goodness arises, and body and mind become pliant. If in the three evil destinies, in places of utmost suffering, they see this light, all receive rest, and at death they all attain liberation. If any sentient beings, having heard of this light and its majestic virtue, day and night proclaim it with single-mindedness not ceasing, according to their wishes, they are born in that land.

blocks.text: Chapter Thirteen: Immeasurable Life and Multitude

inline.s: The Buddha told Ananda: Amitabha Buddha's life-span is long, beyond reckoning. There are also countless hearers, of penetrating wisdom and free power, able to hold all worlds in the palm of the hand.

Among my disciples, Mahamaudgalyayana is foremost in spiritual powers; in the three thousand great thousand worlds, all the stars and sentient beings, he can know their number in a day and night. Even if the sentient beings of the ten directions all became pratyekabuddhas, each with a life of a koti of years, their powers like Mahamaudgalyayana, and exhausting their lives and their wisdom, they together calculated the number of hearers in that Buddha's assembly, and would not reach a ten-millionth part.

For example, the great ocean is deep, broad, and boundless. Suppose one took a hair, split it into a hundred parts, and ground it into dust. With one particle of that hair-dust, dipping one drop of the ocean: this drop of water compared to the ocean, which is more? Ananda, the number known by Maudgalyayana and such is like the drop of water; the number unknown is like the mighty ocean. The life-span of that Buddha, and of his bodhisattvas, hearers, gods, and humans, is likewise, beyond what calculation and simile can know.
Chapter Fourteen: Treasure Trees Throughout the Land

That Thus-Come One's land has many treasure trees. Some are trees of pure gold, of pure silver, of pure lapis lazuli, of pure crystal, of pure amber, of pure fine jade, of pure agate, made of a single jewel, unmixed with other jewels. Some are of two or three jewels, even up to seven jewels, formed by intermingling. Their roots, trunks, branches, and stems are made of these jewels, while their flowers, leaves, fruits, are transformed from other jewels.

Some treasure trees have gold for their roots, silver for their trunks, lapis lazuli for their branches, crystal for their tips, amber for their leaves, fine jade for their flowers, and agate for their fruit. Other trees further have the seven jewels configured as roots, trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit in manifold combinations.

Each in its own row, row answering row, trunk looking over trunk, branch and leaf facing each other, flower and fruit in mutual correspondence, with brilliant color and radiance beyond gaze. From time to time a pure breeze rises, producing fivefold notes, subtle and harmonious, spontaneously accordant. All these jewel trees fill the land.

blocks.text: Chapter Fifteen: The Bodhimanda of Enlightenment

inline.s: In that bodhimanda there is a bodhi tree, four million li high. Its trunk is five thousand yojanas in girth, branches and leaves spreading four hundred thousand li, naturally formed of all treasures. Flowers and fruit flourish, their light shining everywhere. There are also red, green, blue, and white mani jewels, the kings of gems, as ornaments. Clouds of gathered jewels adorn the jewel pillars. Golden beads and bells (duo) hang among the branches.

A net of precious, wondrous gems is spread over it. In a hundred, a thousand hues, each adorning the other, immeasurable light radiates without end; every adornment appears in accord with conditions. A gentle breeze softly stirs, blowing the branches and leaves, producing immeasurable, wonderful sounds of the Dharma. This sound flows and spreads throughout all Buddha lands. Clear, flowing, and majestic, subtle and harmonious, in the sounds of the worlds of the ten directions, it is the foremost.

If any sentient beings behold the bodhi tree, hear its sound, smell its fragrance, taste its fruit, touch its light and shadow, and reflect on its merit, they all attain clear faculties, without affliction or distress, abiding in non-retrogression until they attain the Buddha Way. Moreover, by seeing that tree, they obtain three kinds of patience: the patience of sound, the patience of compliant acceptance, and the patience of the non-arising of dharmas.

The Buddha told Ananda: In such a Buddha land, flowers, fruit, and trees do the work of Buddha for all sentient beings. This is all because of Amitabha Buddha's power of majesty, his power of original vows, his power of fulfilled vows, and his minds clearly, firmly, and ultimately accomplished.

blocks.text: Chapter Sixteen: Halls, Abodes, and Towers

inline.s: Moreover, the lecture halls, retreats, towers
guan
and railings are all naturally formed of the seven jewels, and there are white pearls and mani gems interwoven, wondrous and incomparable. The palaces where the bodhisattvas abide are likewise.

Among them some on the ground teach the scriptures, some recite them, some receive the scriptures, some listen to them, some walk meditating, reflecting on the Way or sitting in meditation; some in the sky recite, listen, walk meditating, reflect, or sit in meditation.

Some attain the fruit of stream-entry, some of once-return, some of non-return or of arhatship. Those who have not attained non-retrogression then attain it. Each reflecting on the Way, speaking of it, and practicing it, none but rejoice.

blocks.text: Chapter Seventeen: The Merits of the Springs and Pools

inline.s: In the lecture halls and retreats, and within the dwellings of the bodhisattvas and arhats, inside and outside in all places, there are naturally flowing springs and bathing pools. Clear and fragrant, endowed with the eight virtues: first, serene; second, cool; third, sweet; fourth, light and soft; fifth, moistening; sixth, tranquil and harmonious; seventh, in drinking, it dispels thirst and countless other ills; eighth, having drunk, it surely sustains the faculties and the four elements, increasing various supreme roots of good.

When the bodhisattvas and arhats wish to bathe, they each enter the seven-jeweled pools to bathe. They may wish the water to reach the feet, the knees, the waist, the armpits, or the neck; or wish to be sprinkled over the whole body; or wish it cold or warm, rushing or gentle; the water responds to each being's mind. It refreshes the spirit and delights the body, pure as if formless. Jeweled sand shines clearly, and no depth but is illumined. Gentle ripples slowly return, pouring into one another.

Amitabha Buddha's jeweled pools are forty-eight thousand li long and forty-eight thousand li wide. They are all formed by the intermingling of the seven jewels. The sand at the bottom of the pools is of white pearls, moon-bright pearls, and mani gems.

On the banks are sandalwood trees, auspicious-fruit trees, utpala flowers, padma flowers, kumuda flowers, and pundarika flowers; their flowers and fruit are ever fragrant, shining with light. Long branches and dense leaves spread over the water. They give forth various scents beyond anything in the world. Carried by the wind, the fragrance
fu
drifts and flows along the water.

The waves raise immeasurable, subtle sounds; one hears the sound of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, the sound of the perfections, the sound of stilling and cessation, the sound of non-arising and non-ceasing, the sound of the ten powers and the fearlessnesses; one hears the sound of non-self, of no-creation, of no-self-nature, the sound of great compassion, joy, and equanimity, the sound of sweet-dew consecration and the stage of receiving the position. Having heard such various sounds, the mind becomes pure, free of discrimination, upright and equal, maturing roots of good. Whatever one hears accords with the Dharma. What one wishes to hear, one hears
(zhe)
alone; what one does not wish to hear, one hears not at all. Never do they retreat from the mind of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

The beings of the ten directions who are reborn there are all born naturally by transformation in lotus flowers in the jeweled pools. All receive a pure, empty body and an immeasurable form. They do not hear the name of the three evil destinies, or of distress, suffering, and calamity. If such names have not even a name, how much less actual suffering. But there is the sound of natural bliss. Therefore that land is called Sukhavati.

blocks.text: Chapter Eighteen: Wondrous Countenances

inline.s: All the sentient beings of that Sukhavati land have wondrous countenances, surpassing the rare in the world. They are all of one kind, without difference of appearance. But in accordance with the customs of other regions, they are called gods and humans.

The Buddha told Ananda: For example, a poor, suffering beggar in the world, beside an emperor in his sovereignty, can his face and form compare? If the emperor were compared to a wheel-turning sage, he would be base and lowly, like that beggar beside the emperor. A wheel-turning sage, foremost in majestic appearance, compared to a lord of the Trayastrimsa heaven, would again be ugly and inferior. Even a lord of the Trayastrimsa heaven, compared to a lord of the heaven of sovereignty over the bliss of others, a hundred-thousandfold would they not resemble. And a lord of that heaven, if compared to the bodhisattvas and hearers of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, though a koti-fold, would not approach them.

The palaces, clothing, food, and drink they have are like those of the lord of the heaven of sovereignty over the bliss of others. As for majesty, rank, spiritual power, and transformations, all gods and humans cannot compare, a hundred thousand kotis and countless times beyond.
Ananda, you should know that the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitabha Buddha, with such merit and adornment, is inconceivable!

blocks.text: Chapter Nineteen: Fulfillment of Enjoyments

inline.s: Further, all the sentient beings of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, whether already born, now born, or to be born, all obtain such wondrous bodies of form. Their appearance is upright and dignified, their merit and virtue immeasurable. Wisdom is lucid and clear, spiritual power free and at ease. In all their enjoyments, everything is abundant. Palaces, garments, fragrant flowers, banners, and canopies, ornaments, whatever they require, all come as their thoughts wish.

When they wish to eat, the seven-jeweled bowls appear of themselves before them, filled with a hundred flavors. Though there is this food, in truth there is no eater. They merely see its color and smell its fragrance, taking it as their food by thought; their color and strength increase, and yet no waste or impurity. Body and mind become pliant, without attachment to taste. When the meal is over, it vanishes, and reappears when the time comes.
There are also wondrous garments of many treasures, caps, girdles, and ornaments, with immeasurable light and a hundred thousand subtle hues, all complete, naturally on their bodies.

The dwellings they live in are as their hearts desire. Jewel nets cover them, jewel bells hang from them. Fine and rare, wonderful and precious, everywhere adorned. Their radiance is dazzling, surpassing in splendor. Towers, rails, palaces, halls, chambers, wide and narrow, square and round, great or small, some in the sky, some on the ground, pure, stable, and wondrously blissful. They appear as thoughts arise, and nothing is lacking.

blocks.text: Chapter Twenty: The Virtuous Wind and Rain of Flowers

inline.s: In that Buddha land, at each mealtime, a natural, virtuous wind, soft and gentle, arises and blows upon the jewel nets and the many treasure trees. It produces subtle sounds, preaching suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, and the perfections, spreading a myriad of kinds of mild, elegant, virtuous fragrance. Those who smell it, their weariness of defilements and habits naturally does not arise. The wind touches their bodies, gentle and harmonious, like a monk who has attained the samadhi of cessation.

It further blows upon the seven-jeweled groves, scattering flowers into heaps, of various hues and light, filling the Buddha land. In the order of their colors, not jumbled. Soft and radiant, like kapok cotton. Stepping on them, one sinks four inches, and as the foot lifts, they return to their former state. After the mealtime, the flowers vanish of themselves, and the ground becomes pure. At the proper times, fresh flowers rain again, spreading everywhere once more, the same as before, six times each day.

blocks.text: Chapter Twenty-One: Jeweled Lotuses and Buddha Light

inline.s: Moreover, many jeweled lotuses fill the world. Each jeweled flower has a hundred thousand kotis of petals. Their light is of immeasurable hues. Blue flowers have blue light, white flowers white light; yellow, black, vermilion, and purple, their lights likewise. Further, there are immeasurable wondrous gems, a hundred thousand mani jewels, adorning the rare and precious, bright as sun and moon.

The size of those lotuses is half a yojana, or one, two, three, four, even up to a hundred or a thousand yojanas. From each flower issue thirty-six hundred thousand kotis of rays. From each ray issue thirty-six hundred thousand kotis of Buddhas, their bodies of purple-gold hue, their marks supreme. Each Buddha further emits a hundred thousand rays of light, universally preaching the subtle Dharma in the ten directions. All these Buddhas each establish immeasurable sentient beings upon the Buddha's true Way.

blocks.text: Chapter Twenty-Two: Abiding in the Correct Destiny

inline.s: Further, Ananda, in that Buddha land there is no darkness, no firelight, no sun, moon, or stars, no sign of day or night, no name of years, months, or aeons, and no attachment to home. In all places, there is neither standard of designation nor grasping and rejecting, but only the reception of the purest, supreme bliss.

If good men or good women, whether already born or to be born there, all abide in the destiny of correctness, and will surely realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Why? Because those of the erroneous destiny and the indeterminate destiny cannot understand the establishment of that cause.

blocks.text: Chapter Twenty-Three: Praise by the Buddhas of the Ten Directions

inline.s: Further, Ananda, in the worlds of the eastern Ganges-sands, in each world there are Ganges-sands of Buddhas, each putting forth the broad, long tongue, radiating immeasurable light, and speaking truthful words, praising the inconceivable merit of Amitabha Buddha. The Buddhas of the southern, western, and northern Ganges-sands worlds likewise praise him. The Buddhas of the four directions and above and below, Ganges-sands of them, also praise him in like manner.

Why is this? Because they wish all the sentient beings of other regions, hearing that Buddha's name, to bring forth a pure mind, to remember and uphold it, to take refuge and make offerings. And even to bring forth one thought of pure faith, with all roots of good sincerely dedicated, aspiring to be born in that land. According to their wishes they are all born there, attaining non-retrogression, even to the supreme, perfect enlightenment.

blocks.text: Chapter Twenty-Four: The Three Grades of Rebirth

inline.s: The Buddha told Ananda: The gods and humans of the worlds of the ten directions who sincerely wish to be born in that land are of three grades.

Of the highest grade: they abandon home and desires, become monks, bring forth the bodhi mind, single-mindedly think of Amitabha Buddha, practice various merits, and wish to be born in that land. Such beings, at death, have Amitabha Buddha appear before them with the great assembly, and they follow that Buddha, reborn in his land, born by transformation in a seven-jeweled flower, abiding in non-retrogression, with wisdom, valor, and spiritual freedom. Therefore, Ananda, those who wish in this life to see Amitabha Buddha should bring forth the mind of supreme bodhi, practice merit and virtue, and wish to be born in that land.

Of the middle grade: the gods and humans of the worlds of the ten directions who with sincere mind wish to be born in that land, though unable to become monks and greatly cultivate merit, should bring forth the mind of supreme bodhi, single-mindedly think of Amitabha Buddha, and, more or less, cultivate good. Keeping the precepts and fasting, erecting stupas and images, offering food to monks, hanging silken banners, lighting lamps, scattering flowers, and burning incense, and dedicating this merit, they wish to be born in that land. At their death, Amitabha Buddha manifests his transformed body, with light and marks, complete like the true Buddha, and appears before them with the great assembly. They follow that transformed Buddha, reborn in his land, abiding in non-retrogression; their merit and wisdom are next to those of the highest grade.

Of the lowest grade: the gods and humans of the worlds of the ten directions who with sincere mind wish to be born in that land, though unable to practice various merits, should bring forth the mind of supreme bodhi and with single-minded intent, even with ten thoughts, think of Amitabha Buddha, wishing to be born in his land. There are also beings who, hearing the profound Dharma, rejoice and believe with joy, without doubt, and even with one thought think of that Buddha, and with utmost sincere mind wish to be born in his land. At their death they dream of Amitabha Buddha and are also reborn there; their merit and wisdom are next to those of the middle grade.

blocks.text: Chapter Twenty-Five: The True Causes of Rebirth

inline.s: Further, Ananda, if good men or good women hear this scripture, uphold, read, and recite it, copy it, and make offerings, day and night without ceasing, seeking rebirth in that land; bring forth the bodhi mind, keep all the precepts, and steadfastly observe them; benefit beings, and give away whatever good they have done, causing them to attain peace; remember Amitabha Buddha and his land. These beings at death, with the Buddha's marks and adornments, are born in the jeweled land, quickly hear the Dharma, and never retreat.

Further, Ananda, if beings wish to be born in that land, though unable to practice great diligence in meditation and keep all the precepts perfectly, they should at least do good: first, not to kill; second, not to steal; third, not to commit adultery; fourth, not to speak falsely; fifth, not to speak frivolously; sixth, not to use harsh words; seventh, not to speak double-tongued; eighth, not to be greedy; ninth, not to be angry; tenth, not to be deluded. Thus day and night they reflect on the manifold merits and adornments of Amitabha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. With heartfelt refuge they bow and make offerings. At death, without fear and a confused mind, they are then reborn in that Buddha's land.

If one is much occupied with worldly affairs and cannot leave home, nor find time for great austerities and purity of mind, when there is free time they should rectify body and mind, put away desires and grief, be compassionate and diligent. They should not be angry or envious, nor given to greed (tie) or stinginess (qian). They should not later regret, nor be doubtful.

They should be filial and sincere, upright and faithful. They should believe the scriptures of the Buddha are profound, and believe that doing good brings good fortune. Observing such dharmas, they should not let them be lost. Reflecting carefully and pondering, they wish to attain liberation. Day and night they constantly think, wishing to be reborn in the pure Buddha land of Amitabha Buddha. If they do so for ten days and ten nights, or even for one day and one night, without ceasing, at the end of their lives they are all reborn in that land, practicing the bodhisattva's way.

All those reborn there attain non-retrogression, all have true gold-colored bodies with the thirty-two marks, and all shall become Buddhas. Wherever in the Buddha lands they wish to become Buddhas, according to their mind's wish. According to their diligence, seeking the Way day and night without rest, they will certainly attain it, and not lose what they wish.
Ananda, because of this benefit, immeasurable, countless, inconceivable, and boundless worlds beyond compare — the Thus-Come Ones of them all together praise all the merits of Amitabha Buddha.

blocks.text: Chapter Twenty-Six: Repairs to the Land of Ultimate Bliss

inline.s: Further, Ananda, the hosts of bodhisattvas of the worlds of the ten directions, wishing to worship the Land of Ultimate Bliss and Amitabha Buddha, each with fragrant flowers, banners, and jewelled canopies, go to the place of Buddha. With respect they make offerings, hear the scriptures and Dharma, proclaim the Way, and praise the merit and adornment of the Buddha land.
Then the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
The Buddha lands of the east, numberless as the Ganges-sands, with Ganges-sands of bodhisattva hosts, repair to pay homage to Immeasurable Life.
South, west, north, the four directions, above and below likewise, all with reverent hearts, offer precious, wondrous gifts.
They raise harmonious, gentle voices, singing praise to the most supreme; thoroughly reaching transcendent wisdom, they enter the deep Dharma door.
Hearing the sage's name of virtue, they gain a great and stable benefit; amid all manner of offerings they practice diligently, never weary.
They behold that supreme land, subtle and beyond thought; adorned with universal merit, beyond the Buddha lands, they bring forth the mind of the supreme, wishing speedily to attain bodhi.

At that moment the Immeasurable Honored One smiled, and his golden countenance shone; light issued from his mouth, illumining the lands of the ten directions, then returning to circle the Buddha, three times, entering the crown of his head.
The bodhisattvas, seeing this light, at once realized the stage of non-retrogression; the whole assembly rejoiced and congratulated one another that joy arose.
The Buddha's words resounded like thunder, in the eight tones of sweet melody.
The true sages come from the ten directions; I know all their vows, seeking to adorn a pure land, and shall receive the prophecy of becoming Buddhas.
Having realized all dharmas are like a dream, an echo, a phantom, fulfilling all their wondrous vows, they must accomplish such a land.
Knowing the land is like an image, they ever arouse great vows, fulfill the bodhisattva's path, endow all roots of merit, cultivate the supreme bodhi course, and receive the prophecy of Buddhahood.
Penetrating the nature of all dharmas, all empty and selfless, single-mindedly seeking a pure Buddha land, they must accomplish such a land.
Hearing the Dharma, joyfully they practice, arriving at the pure abode; before the Immeasurable Honored One they receive the prophecy and attain perfect enlightenment.
That boundless, supreme land, by that Buddha's original vow, hearing the name and wishing to be reborn, of itself arrives at non-retrogression.

The bodhisattvas raise the utmost vow, wishing their own land to be like this, thinking universally to deliver all, each bringing forth the bodhi mind, renouncing the body of samsara, and causing all to reach the other shore.

blocks.text: Chapter Twenty-Seven: Making Offerings to the Buddhas

inline.s: The Buddha told Ananda: The bodhisattvas of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, by the Buddha's majestic power, within the space of a single meal, repair to the boundless pure lands of the ten directions to make offerings to the Buddhas. Fragrant flowers, banners, and canopies, their offering implements, come at their thought and appear in their hands. Fine, wondrous, and supreme, not of this world, they present them to the Buddhas and the hosts of bodhisattvas.

The flowers they scatter combine in the sky into a single flower. All the flowers face downward, round and orderly, forming flower canopies. With a hundred thousand hues and various fragrances, the perfume spreads everywhere. The smallest canopy covers ten yojanas; increasing manifold, until it covers the three thousand great thousand worlds. According to their order, they vanish in turn. If new flowers are not scattered again, the former flowers never fall. In the sky they together play heavenly music, praising the Buddha's virtues in subtle sound.

Within a moment they return to their own land and all assemble in the seven-jeweled lecture hall. Amitabha Buddha then proclaims the great teaching broadly, expounding the subtle Dharma. None but rejoice, and their minds are freed, attaining the Way.

At that moment a fragrant wind blows the seven-jeweled trees, producing the fivefold sound. Immeasurable wondrous flowers scatter in the four directions with the wind, naturally making offerings, not ceasing. All the devas bring
ji

a hundred thousand fragrant flowers and myriad kinds of music, making offerings to that Buddha and the hosts of bodhisattvas and hearers. They come and go, tranquil and joyous. This is all because of Amitabha Buddha's original vows and added power, and their former offerings to the Thus-Come One, with roots of good continuing without decrease, because of their excellent practice, excellent acceptance, and excellent accomplishment.

blocks.text: Chapter Twenty-Eight: Avalokitesvara and Mahasthamaprapta

inline.s: The Buddha told Ananda: The hosts of bodhisattvas in that Buddha land all clearly see and hear the affairs of the eight directions, above and below, past, future, and present. Of gods and humans, even of the flitting and wriggling creatures, the good and evil of their minds, the words their mouths wish to speak, and when they shall be delivered, attain the Way, and be reborn there, they all know beforehand.

Moreover, the hearers of that Buddha land have body-lights of one fathom; the light of the bodhisattvas illumines a hundred yojanas. There are two bodhisattvas, most honored and supreme, whose majestic light shines throughout the three thousand great thousand worlds.
Ananda asked the Buddha: What are the names of those two bodhisattvas?

The Buddha said: One named Avalokitesvara, one named Mahasthamaprapta. These two bodhisattvas, in this Saha world, practiced the bodhisattva's course, and reborn in that land, always dwell at the left and right of Amitabha Buddha. When they wish to go to the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions, they reach them as their minds wish. Now dwelling in this world, they bring great benefit and joy. Good men and good women of the world, if they have urgent distress and fear, only by taking refuge in Avalokitesvara bodhisattva, none fail to be released.

blocks.text: Chapter Twenty-Nine: Attaining the Stage of One More Birth

inline.s: Further, Ananda, all the bodhisattvas of that Buddha land, whether present or future, shall ultimately reach the stage of one more birth. Except those of great vow who enter the world of birth and death to deliver beings, roaring the lion's roar; donning
huan
the great armor
zhou, helmet

, they adorn themselves with the merit of the great vows. Though born in the five defilements of an evil age, they manifest like those there, yet until they become Buddhas, they do not enter the evil destinies; in every place of birth, they always know their past lives.

Amitabha Buddha wishes to deliver the sentient beings of the worlds of the ten directions, causing them all to be reborn in his land, and all to attain the Way of nirvana; those who are bodhisattvas, he causes all to become Buddhas. Having become Buddhas, they in turn teach and deliver one another, and so on without cease, beyond counting.

The hearers, bodhisattvas, and all sorts of sentient beings of the worlds of the ten directions, born in that Buddha land, attain the Way of nirvana and shall become Buddhas beyond number. In that Buddha land it is ever like a single Dharma, not increasing more and more. Why? Just as the great ocean is the king of waters, and all rivers flow into it, does this great ocean water increase?

The Buddha lands of the eight directions, above and below, are countless. The Land of Ultimate Bliss is lasting and vast, bright, good, and blissful, most supremely excellent. It is due to the merits accumulated when he was a bodhisattva seeking the Way and the vows of his practice. Amitabha Buddha's grace and generosity spread through the eight directions, above and below, without end, deep, great, and immeasurable, beyond full expression.

blocks.text: Chapter Thirty: The Practice and Sustaining of the Bodhisattvas

inline.s: Further, Ananda, all the bodhisattvas of that Buddha land, in meditation, wisdom, spiritual power, and majestic virtue, are all perfect. The profound treasury of the Buddhas they understand fully. They tame their faculties, and body and mind become pliant. They enter deep true wisdom, without remaining habits. In accord with the Buddha's practice, they rely on the seven factors of enlightenment and the noble eightfold path.

Their eloquence and dharani are free and unhindered. Skillfully they understand the boundless expedient means of the world. Their words are true and sincere, penetrating the flavor of truth. They deliver sentient beings, preaching the true Dharma: without characteristics, without acting, without bondage, without release; without discrimination, far from inversion. In all they receive and use, they have no grasping or attachment.

They roam throughout the Buddha lands, without attachment or aversion. They have no thoughts of seeking or not seeking, no thoughts of self and other, or of enmity. Why? Because those bodhisattvas, toward all sentient beings, have a heart of great compassion and benefit. They forsake all clinging and accomplish immeasurable merit and virtue.
